contentBlocks.body: TypeScript lets some declarations with the same name combine into one. The most common case is interface merging: two interface declarations with the same name in the same scope become a single interface with the members of both. This is the main practical difference between interface and type: a type alias with a duplicate name is simply an error.

Merging is what makes augmentation possible: adding members to types you do not own. Global augmentation extends built-in or global types from inside a module with declare global. Module augmentation reopens a library's exported interface with declare module "library-name", which is how libraries let you register your own types.

Namespaces, functions, classes, and enums can also merge in specific combinations. For example, a function and a namespace with the same name let you attach typed properties to a function. You will mostly meet these in library type definitions rather than write them yourself.
Augmentation only changes types. Declaring window.appVersion does not create it; your code still has to assign it at runtime, or reads will return undefined while the compiler says string.

An augmentation file must be included by tsconfig (for example through include or typeRoots) or the compiler never sees it. If a module augmentation seems to be ignored, check that the file is a module (has an import or export) and that the module name matches exactly.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Two declarations interface A { x: number } and interface A { y: string } appear in the same file. What is A?

choices: one interface with both x and y
payload.answer: one interface with both x and y
payload.explanation: Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge their members.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What happens with type T = { a: string } followed by type T = { b: string }?

payload.explanation: Type aliases never merge; only interfaces (and certain namespace, class, function, and enum combinations) do.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Which construct adds a property to the global Window interface from inside a module file?

payload.explanation: declare global reopens global declarations from a module, and the interfaces merge.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why must an augmentation file like globals.d.ts contain export {} or an import?

choices: to export the types to other files
declare global and module augmentation are only allowed in module files
to make the file run at startup
payload.answer: declare global and module augmentation are only allowed in module files
payload.explanation: A file with no import or export is a global script; the augmentation syntax requires a module.

knowledgeItems.prompt: After augmenting Express's Request with user?, what is req.user at runtime if no middleware sets it?

payload.explanation: Augmentation only affects types; something at runtime must still assign the property.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Two merged interfaces declare the same property with different types. What happens?

payload.explanation: Non-function members must have identical types across merged declarations. Methods with different signatures become overloads instead.

payload.text: declare ____ "express-serve-static-core" { interface Request { user?: User } } adds a property to a library interface.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Model the compiler: merge interface declarations by name and report the error for conflicting property types.
